Consumers – All animals are called as consumers because they depend on plants for their food. They are heterotrophs. They are categorized into following groups: i. Primary consumer: These organisms fully depend upon the producer for food. e.g. rat, rabbit, dear etc. ii. Secondary consumer: These organisms depend upon the primary consumer for food. e.g. insects, frog, small fishes etc. iii. Tertiary consumer: These organisms depend upon the secondary consumer for food. e.g. tiger, lion, snake, big fish etc. c. Decomposers – They obtain their food from dead and decaying body of organism. They convert the complex organic matter of dead and decaying matter into simple inorganic compounds. It includes bacteria and fungi.
4.1.3 SPECIES INTERACTION

The living organisms of an ecosystem form a biotic community. All the organism of a particular habitat influences each other directly or indirectly. Interaction is a necessity for any living being to survive. They can be either of the same species (intraspecific interactions), or of different species (interspecific interactions).
1. Positive Interaction
It is the type of interaction in which one or both partners are benefited and no one is harmed.

a. Mutualism (Symbiosis): It is the biotic interaction between two organisms of different species where both partners are benefited. The relationship is obligatory (i.e. they can not survive independently). Example: Rhizobium bacteria and leguminous plant, mycorrhiza etc.

b. Commensalism: It is the biotic interaction between two organisms of different species where one partner is benefitted and other is neither benefited nor harmed. Example: epiphytes, Sucker fish and shark etc.

c. Protocooperation: It is the biotic interaction between two organisms of different species where both partners are benefited but the relationship is not obligatory. Example: Flower and insect, birds and cattle etc.
d. Colonization: It is the grouping of individuals of same species for better protection and food. Example: Volvox, Nostoc etc.
e. Social Organization: It is the grouping of individuals of same species that show the division of labour. Example: honey bee, wasp, ants etc.
2. Negative interaction:

It is the type of interaction in which one partner is benefited and other is harmed. a. Parasitism: It is the interaction in which one organism, the parasite is benefited while the other organism, the host, is harmed. Example: mosquito and human, leech and cattle, etc.

b. Predation: It is the interaction in which one organism kills and feeds on the other. Here one partner is benefited and other is harmed. Example: tiger and deer, frog and insect etc.
c. Competition: It is the interaction between similar or different species for food, support, shelter, space etc. Here either of the organisms is harmed. Example: Lichens, herbs, birds etc.

4.1.4 CONCEPT OF ECOSYSTEM In nature an organism does not exist in isolation, it is associated with organisms of its own and of different kinds as well as with the physical environment. If the organism is plant, it depends for growth on the aerial environment for light, temperature and carbon dioxide, on the soil environment for inorganic nutrients and water. If it is an animal it depends on the plants for food and shelter. If it is a microorganism it depend on the dead organic matter from plants and animals for its food, and releases the nutrients tied in the organic matter for the reuse of plants. Thus, there are continuous interactions among the organisms and between the organisms and the habitat resulting into an integrated, functional unit. This functional unit is known as ecosystem. It is the structural and functional unit of ecology. Thus, ecosystem is defined as ‘the structural and functional unit of ecology where the living organisms interact with each other and the surrounding environment’. The term ecosystem was coined by A.G. Tansley (1935). Ecosystem varies greatly in size from a small pond to a large forest or a sea. The ecosystem is divided into two basic categories: Aquatic Ecosystem and Terrestrial Ecosystem. Forest, grassland etc. are terrestrial ecosystem while pond, lake, river etc. are aquatic ecosystem.
STRUCTURAL AND FUNCTIONAL ASPECT OF POND ECOSYSTEM
Ponds are fresh water ecosystem. It is a small reservoir which may or may not dry up during dry season. It is self-sustaining and self-regulating.
Pond ecosystem consists of structural and functional components.
Structural components Structural components are categorized into two main components: Abiotic component and Biotic component.
A. Abiotic component: Abiotic components of pond ecosystem are non-living things of pond and consist of water, dissolved minerals, oxygen, carbon dioxide, solar energy etc.
